The $67 Million Missile: America’s Hypersonic Speed Trap

The Pentagon has demonstrated a new generation of high-speed weapons, but an expensive and troubled production line raises questions about how many it can field.

Alan Tang

Published on this site October 11, 2026

In April 2025, a conventional hypersonic missile thundered into the Florida sky above Cape Canaveral. Compressed gas expelled it from a ground-based launcher before its rocket motor ignited—an approach designed to allow ignition at a safe distance from future naval launch platforms. For the U.S. Navy, the test marked an important advance in Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS), a program designed to hit distant, heavily defended targets with nonnuclear weapons traveling at hypersonic speed.

The test advanced the Navy’s plans for sea-based deployment, but the harder industrial challenge lay in producing enough missiles to make the capability useful beyond a handful of launches.

In July 2026, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that the shared missile-body production line could turn out, at most, six or seven rounds a year—far short of its target of twelve. The Navy’s April 2026 estimate put the average cost of a CPS missile at approximately $67 million. Behind those figures lay an unexpectedly prosaic collection of troubles: difficult protective coatings, more labor than anticipated, and assembly instructions that officials considered impractical for some of the workers expected to follow them.

These problems have acquired new urgency amid the war with Iran, where the rapid expenditure of missiles and air-defense interceptors has exposed the importance of replenishment. The experience has brought a neglected measure of military power into focus: the number of precision weapons a country can replace after it has used them. Against that standard, the CPS production bottleneck looks particularly consequential.

The Weapon That Two Services Share

Hypersonic flight is not new, nor is it synonymous with a revolutionary weapon. Traditional ballistic missiles already reach speeds exceeding Mach 5. The distinctive promise of a modern boost-glide weapon lies in what happens after its rocket carries it upward: a glide vehicle separates, descends through the atmosphere, and maneuvers along a less predictable path than a conventional ballistic trajectory. That maneuverability can complicate defenses, even if it does not make the weapon impossible to intercept. The GAO’s description of CPS identifies precisely this combination of speed, reach, and maneuverability as the system’s attraction.

The Navy intends to field CPS aboard Zumwalt-class destroyers and later certain Virginia-class submarines. The Army plans to fire its version, the Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (LRHW), also known as Dark Eagle, from mobile launchers on land. Both services rely on a common missile and glide body, with Lockheed Martin responsible for missile integration and Dynetics for the common glide body. Their launch approaches differ: the Army uses a ground-based launcher, while the Navy’s cold-gas method ejects the missile before motor ignition.

Sharing a design should, in principle, spare the Pentagon the cost of developing two separate weapons. However, it also creates a shared vulnerability. A delay at the missile or glide-body factory affects both services, regardless of whether the eventual launcher sits on a road or a warship.

The Army originally hoped to field its first complete LRHW battery in fiscal year 2023. It had delivered the ground equipment to soldiers in 2021, but the missile proved harder to bring into service. A June 2025 GAO assessment described four attempted tests in 2023 and 2024 that could not be completed because of problems involving launchers, launch sequences, and missile-production quality. Although a successful end-to-end flight in late 2024 allowed work on the first eight missiles to resume, the program remained behind its original deployment schedule following repeated testing and production setbacks.

The Factory Floor

The most revealing details in the July 2026 GAO investigation were not about exotic aerodynamics. They came from the production line.

Hypersonic vehicles endure severe heating and mechanical stresses. Their components and protective coatings must be manufactured consistently, not merely designed to work in theory. GAO identified quality challenges involving thermal-protection coatings and reported that some production tasks required substantially more labor than planned. Certain technical details were withheld from the public report as controlled unclassified information.

Other obstacles required no knowledge of high-speed flight to understand. Officials found that some assembly instructions resembled engineering specifications more than usable directions for technicians. Army and Navy representatives questioned whether workers arriving from high school or vocational training could reasonably be expected to interpret them as written. The contractor began rewriting instructions across its workstations.

This was a different kind of engineering challenge: turning specialized knowledge into work that can be performed reliably, by a trained workforce, over and over again. A weapon whose manufacture depends on extraordinary intervention at every stage is difficult to produce in ordinary quantities.

The response to the bottleneck also exposed divided responsibilities. GAO reported that the Army spent about $6 million in fiscal year 2025 on a consultant’s examination of the shared missile-body production line. The consultant recommended changes aimed at reaching twelve rounds annually, and Lockheed Martin began implementing some of them. Navy officials, however, questioned elements of the consultant’s analysis and sent their own teams to investigate. Officials also cited contractual limits on how directly the government could dictate the contractor’s manufacturing methods.

Although the services chose a common missile, they continued to manage many of the investments behind its production separately. GAO concluded that the Pentagon lacked a comprehensive strategy for coordinating decisions across the programs that must work together to field CPS.

The Price of Speed

Those manufacturing constraints also sharpen the question of cost. According to GAO’s July 2026 report, the Navy’s estimated CPS life-cycle costs rose from about $31 billion in 2020, based on a planning quantity of 262 missiles, to roughly $41 billion in 2024 for a planning quantity of 224. These are program life-cycle estimates—not simply the cost of buying the missiles—and the quantities were planning assumptions rather than approved inventory requirements.

By April 2026, estimated unit costs ranged from $63 million to $71 million per missile, averaging approximately $67 million. The approximately $67 million average estimate captures the cost of an individual missile, rather than the broader infrastructure needed to produce and launch it. The price might be justified if the weapon can defeat a target that cheaper munitions cannot reach. But the calculation changes when commanders need not one exceptional strike, but dozens of repeatable ones.

The cost extends to the ships being modified to carry the missile. The Zumwalt-class destroyer program was originally envisioned as a fleet of thirty-two, but only three ships were built, amid escalating costs and changing Navy plans. Their mission subsequently shifted, and in 2022 the Navy selected the class as the first host for CPS. Installing the system requires large vertical launch tubes and extensive changes to the vessels.

The GAO found that the estimated price of modernizing all three ships rose from $1.8 billion to at least $2 billion. USS Zumwalt was 94 percent through its modernization as of January 2026, yet unexpected work had pushed it behind schedule. In August 2025, the Navy added some 230,000 labor hours at a cost of $20 million, partly because installing the missile tubes required more electrical cabling work than expected. Shipboard flight testing, once planned for 2025, had moved to 2027.

The Pentagon was paying not only to perfect a missile but to rework the industrial and naval machinery required to use it. A weapon designed to shorten the time between launch and impact was taking years longer to reach its launcher.

What the War with Iran Reveals

The war with Iran offers a stark comparison, although it involves different weapons and missions. Since U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026, the conflict has consumed large quantities of precision weapons and defensive interceptors. According to congressional testimony summarized by the Congressional Research Service, U.S. Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper said American forces conducted more than 13,500 strikes in the first 38 days of major combat operations. According to that testimony, U.S. forces and regional partners also intercepted more than 6,000 one-way attack drones and 1,500 ballistic missiles during that period.

In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that replacing U.S. munitions expended through August 1 would cost $21.7 billion: $13.1 billion for missile-defense interceptors, $7.3 billion for land-attack cruise missiles, and $1.2 billion for other munitions. Certain interceptor inventories, the agency estimated, would probably take at least five years to replenish even at higher production rates. The estimates rely in part on publicly available information about expenditure quantities, rather than complete Pentagon data. The Defense Department’s inspector general also reported that wartime expenditures had exposed inventory shortfalls and industrial bottlenecks. Defense officials have meanwhile maintained publicly that sufficient munitions remain available.

Iran’s use of one-way attack drones adds an asymmetry to that picture: comparatively inexpensive systems can force defenders to make repeated choices about using scarcer, costlier interceptors. But a price comparison is incomplete without accounting for the lives, bases, or infrastructure an interception might protect. An expensive interceptor that saves lives or prevents the destruction of critical infrastructure may be worth every dollar.

CPS is an offensive strike weapon, not an air-defense interceptor, so the Iran experience cannot establish whether it is cost-effective. What the conflict makes clear is that even sophisticated weapons must be evaluated in the context of available inventories, replacement times, and the demands of sustained operations. A uniquely capable weapon may earn its place in the arsenal; it cannot earn that place on speed alone.

That reality reaches beyond hypersonics. A July 2024 GAO study found that four of six offensive hypersonic development efforts had not fully incorporated leading digital-engineering practices, while four had not consistently brought prospective users into early design decisions. In June 2025, GAO reported that major U.S. defense acquisition programs took almost twelve years, on average, to deliver an initial capability. Hypersonic manufacturing difficulties sit inside a wider problem of turning promising designs into usable equipment quickly.

The Real Race

American flight tests demonstrate substantial scientific and engineering progress, and a limited inventory of highly capable conventional weapons may still serve valuable missions. Yet those achievements coexist with production constraints that determine how frequently the capability can be used.

Fielding that capability depends on less visible achievements: coatings applied consistently, technicians equipped with usable instructions, suppliers able to deliver parts, ships ready to accept the weapons, and production lines capable of replenishing what military operations consume.

In July 2026, GAO counted at least $50 billion in planned investments across the related Army and Navy efforts, yet found no comprehensive Pentagon strategy for coordinating the major decisions needed to deliver their shared weapon. That is an industrial and organizational problem, not a failure of imagination.

The hypersonic race is often described as a contest over which country can send a missile through the atmosphere fastest. The ongoing war with Iran, and the Pentagon’s own manufacturing record, paint a less glamorous picture of military strength: how many usable weapons can leave the factory, and how quickly the next ones can follow.

Historically, the United States has invested heavily in reducing the time its missiles need to reach a target. The durability of that advantage will also depend on reducing the time its factories need to produce the next one.
